args.text: folded: a fifth of the footprint

renderSubtitles.text:
Why are cells so small? It comes down to geometry.
Start with a cube, one unit on a side.

Six faces of one square each: surface 6.
Volume 1. Surface to volume: 6.

Double the side: each face is 4 squares, so
surface 24. Volume 8. Surface to volume: 3.

Triple it: each face is 9 squares, so surface
54. Volume 27. Surface to volume: 2.

Surface grows with the square of the side, volume with the cube. So the
bigger it is, the less skin it has for each bit of inside.

A cell lives through its skin: food and oxygen come in,
waste goes out. Too big, and the middle starves.

So cells divide. Cut the big cube into slabs,
then bars, then 27 small cubes.

The volume is still 27, but the surface is now
162. Surface to volume: 6 again.

Life uses this trick everywhere. Inside a
mitochondrion, folds called cristae pack in membrane.

In the lungs, millions of tiny alveoli give a
surface of about 70 square metres.

Small, or folded: that is how living
things get enough surface.
